headline: Two serious security flaws in PHP, the software behind many of the world's websites
deck: PHP is the software that WordPress and millions of other websites run on. A fix came out on 21 October 2026. Government cyber agencies have told organisations to install it now; the two US agencies add: take websites offline if you cannot. Phones and personal computers are not affected.

now.text: A fix has been available since 21 October. Organisations that run websites on PHP are installing it.

Every government cyber agency says: install the fix now. If you cannot, the US agencies say take the website offline; the UK puts that after temporary mitigations, and several European agencies say cut it off from the public internet first.

Attackers are trying to use the flaws, in large numbers: millions of attempts by one internet security company's count. As of 16:05 UTC on 24 October, no named organisation has said it was broken into through this flaw. The one security company that had claimed a successful break-in, Sophos, withdrew it; US banks and the large crypto platforms report none.
The advice is moving from 'install the fix' to 'and check whether you were already broken into'. Singapore's and Luxembourg's authorities now say so.

Some organisations took websites offline as a precaution: the Dutch government took its cyber agency's own site offline, and Dutch press reported the DigiD login down too. Almost all of them are back.

unknown: Whether any website was actually broken into before it installed the fix.

Whether the fix is complete. A report on 21 October suggested it may not be; the PHP security team replied on the mailing list on 22 October, and this site will settle the question once that reply is saved here. Separately, on 23 October PHP published an advisory for another flaw, CVE-2026-115560, which affects fully patched releases and needs a rare session setting (reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News).
Who leaked the news on 20 October, and where.

How many websites went offline, and why. The reports this site holds range from a single site to a whole government's platform; a community tracker lists about fifty sites that went dark and came back. Nobody has counted them all.
Where the 70% figure comes from. None of the pages that use it says how it was measured.

facts.text: There are two flaws. Both are in PHP itself, underneath every website that uses it, and both are rated critical: 9.2 out of 10.

Someone anywhere on the internet, with no password, can use them against a website that has not installed the fix, and make its server run their own commands. Researchers proved this on the most traditional way of running PHP; for other setups it is likely but less certain.
The fix is in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, released on 21 October 2026. Websites on PHP 8.1 or older have no ready-made fix.
The weak spot was first noticed in 2024 and left alone, because nobody could show it was dangerous. In August 2026, three research teams using AI tools showed that it was, and told the PHP project.
The plan was to announce the fix on 22 October. Word leaked out on 20 October, so it was released a day early.

Attackers are trying, in large numbers: one internet security company reports millions of attempts, and Amazon reports a decoy server hit four days before the announcement. No named organisation has said it was broken into through these flaws, as of 16:05 UTC on 24 October, and the US government's official list of flaws known to be used in attacks did not include them when last checked.

Every agency says install the fix. They disagree on what to do if you cannot: the US says take the website offline, the UK lists that as a last resort, several European agencies say cut it off from the public internet, and some say nothing about it.

The headline '70% of the Internet' is not what it sounds like. It is roughly the share of websites whose server-side language is known that use PHP, which is what the same company's own article says; nobody has measured how many are actually at risk.

personas.label: Curious reader
personas.answer: Two serious holes were found in PHP, software that runs on the servers behind a large share of websites. They were fixed on 21 October 2026. Your phone and laptop are not the target: websites are, and it is the job of whoever runs them to update. Some sites were taken offline as a precaution. As of 16:05 UTC on 24 October, the latest capture in the evidence vault, no named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell.

personas.label: Website owner
personas.answer: If your website runs on WordPress, Drupal, Joomla or anything else written in PHP, it is in scope: the flaw is in PHP itself, underneath your site. Updating plugins does not fix it. If someone hosts the site for you, ask them in writing whether PHP has been updated to a fixed version and restarted. If you run the server yourself, update PHP today.

personas.label: Board member or executive
personas.answer: A critical flaw in software that runs many websites, fixed on 21 October. Every agency says update first; some say take systems offline if you cannot. As of 16:05 UTC on 24 October, the latest capture in the evidence vault, no named organisation has said it was broken into through this flaw, though attempts are widespread. Your questions are: do we know every system running PHP, are they updated and restarted, and who can pull a system offline and how fast.

personas.label: Project or programme manager
personas.answer: Expect unplanned work this week: updating PHP on every system that uses it, restarting, and re-testing. Some teams may take systems offline for hours as a precaution. Anything still on PHP 8.1 or older has no ready-made fix and becomes a migration project. Ask each system owner for a patch date and a test plan.

personas.label: CFO
personas.answer: The documented cost so far is precaution, not breach: hours to a day of downtime for organisations that pulled sites, and engineering time to update. As of 16:05 UTC on 24 October, the latest capture in the evidence vault, no named organisation has said it was compromised through this flaw. Ask your broker now, in writing, whether a precautionary shutdown with no breach is covered. Do not use 70% of the Internet in any forecast.

personas.label: Data protection officer
personas.answer: A flaw is not a breach. An unpatched, internet-facing PHP application holding personal data is a risk to record and treat; it becomes a breach to assess when there is a sign of compromise on it. No named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell as of the last check. Ask your hosts in writing, review from 17 October, and document the assessment either way.

personas.label: CISO
personas.answer: The flaw is in the PHP runtime, so exposure is every internet-facing system running PHP, including vendor appliances. Review logs from 17 October (the earliest reported attempt), not from the fix. Attempts are reported at scale; no named victim is confirmed. Patch first, isolate where you cannot.

personas.label: CTO
personas.answer: Patch internet-facing mod_php first, then FPM, then the rest; restart every worker and rebuild every image. The fix changes how PHP behaves when memory runs out, so test under load. 7.4 to 8.1 have no release. Afterwards, invest in an inventory that answers 'where is PHP' in minutes.

personas.label: Journalist
personas.answer: The 70% figure is a share of websites that use PHP, restated as a share of the Internet. The release was 21 October, not 22. Three parties claim the discovery; their dates do not conflict, their framing does. No agency has confirmed a successful compromise, and CISA has not listed either flaw as exploited.

personas.label: Communications team
personas.answer: Safe to say: two critical flaws in PHP were fixed on 21 October; we updated or isolated our systems; we have no evidence of compromise and review continues. Do not say '70% of the Internet', 'the most severe ever' or 'exploited everywhere'. Point people to php.net and your national agency.

personas.label: Security lead
personas.answer: Internet-facing mod_php first, then FPM, then everything else. Where patching slips, apply php.net's temporary settings and record that each blocks a known path only. Alert on PHP workers spawning shells or fetching tools. Decide now who calls isolate or offline, and when.

personas.label: Head of AppSec
personas.answer: Every application on an affected runtime is in scope, including ones with no uploads or sessions: the demonstrated paths run before application code. Add the running PHP version to the SBOM and fail the pipeline on an unfixed one. Detection belongs at the edge and on the host, not in the app.

personas.label: PHP or platform engineer
personas.answer: Target 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35; restart every worker and rebuild images. Until then: session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or the pool, low post_max_size, fatal_error_backtraces=0 on 8.5, pm.max_requests=1 on FPM. Verify with php -v inside the running container. Keep session.upload_progress.enabled=0 after the update as well: CVE-2026-115560, published by PHP on 23 October (as Cloudflare and SOCRadar report), affects the fixed releases under a rare session setting and is fixed only in the next regular release.

personas.label: Developer
personas.answer: Your code is not the problem and cannot be the fix: the flaw is in the engine beneath it. ini_set, .user.ini and auto_prepend_file all run too late. Check the running version where the code runs, after the restart, and tell the platform owner today if your target is 8.1 or older.

personas.label: Security researcher
personas.answer: Two classes: an out-of-memory longjmp leaving request memory uninitialised, and worker global state pointing at freed request memory across requests. mod_php was exploited before application code; FPM for the first flaw is disputed. The fix removes longjmp for OOM. A report of an incomplete fix is open.

personas.label: Analyst or policy advisor
personas.answer: A bug class seen and shelved in 2024 was turned into working exploits by three AI-assisted teams within three weeks in August 2026. The disclosure leaked 22.5 hours early. Agencies split on the hardest question, offline or not, along lines that look institutional rather than technical.

items.title: Briefing: CISO
items.text: The flaw is in the PHP runtime, so exposure is every internet-facing system running PHP, including vendor appliances. Review logs from 17 October (the earliest reported attempt), not from the fix. Attempts are reported at scale; no named victim is confirmed. Patch first, isolate where you cannot.

items.title: Briefing: CTO
items.text: Patch internet-facing mod_php first, then FPM, then the rest; restart every worker and rebuild every image. The fix changes how PHP behaves when memory runs out, so test under load. 7.4 to 8.1 have no release. Afterwards, invest in an inventory that answers 'where is PHP' in minutes.

items.title: Briefing: CFO
items.text: The documented cost so far is precaution, not breach: hours to a day of downtime for organisations that pulled sites, and engineering time to update. As of 16:05 UTC on 24 October, the latest capture in the evidence vault, no named organisation has said it was compromised through this flaw. Ask your broker now, in writing, whether a precautionary shutdown with no breach is covered. Do not use 70% of the Internet in any forecast.

items.title: Briefing: Head of AppSec
items.text: Every application on an affected runtime is in scope, including ones with no uploads or sessions: the demonstrated paths run before application code. Add the running PHP version to the SBOM and fail the pipeline on an unfixed one. Detection belongs at the edge and on the host, not in the app.

items.title: Briefing: Developer
items.text: Your code is not the problem and cannot be the fix: the flaw is in the engine beneath it. ini_set, .user.ini and auto_prepend_file all run too late. Check the running version where the code runs, after the restart, and tell the platform owner today if your target is 8.1 or older.

items.title: Briefing: Media and communications team
items.text: Safe to say: two critical flaws in PHP were fixed on 21 October; we updated or isolated our systems; we have no evidence of compromise and review continues. Do not say '70% of the Internet', 'the most severe ever' or 'exploited everywhere'. Point people to php.net and your national agency.

items.title: Briefing: Curious reader
items.text: Two serious holes were found in PHP, software that runs on the servers behind a large share of websites. They were fixed on 21 October 2026. Your phone and laptop are not the target: websites are, and it is the job of whoever runs them to update. Some sites were taken offline as a precaution. As of 16:05 UTC on 24 October, the latest capture in the evidence vault, no named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell.

items.title: Briefing: Website owner
items.text: If your website runs on WordPress, Drupal, Joomla or anything else written in PHP, it is in scope: the flaw is in PHP itself, underneath your site. Updating plugins does not fix it. If someone hosts the site for you, ask them in writing whether PHP has been updated to a fixed version and restarted. If you run the server yourself, update PHP today.

items.title: Briefing: Project or programme manager
items.text: Expect unplanned work this week: updating PHP on every system that uses it, restarting, and re-testing. Some teams may take systems offline for hours as a precaution. Anything still on PHP 8.1 or older has no ready-made fix and becomes a migration project. Ask each system owner for a patch date and a test plan.

items.title: Front page: right now
items.text: A fix has been available since 21 October. Organisations that run websites on PHP are installing it. Every government cyber agency says: install the fix now. If you cannot, the US agencies say take the website offline; the UK puts that after temporary mitigations, and several European agencies say cut it off from the public internet first.

items.title: Front page: at a glance
items.text: Is there a fix?: Yes (install PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35). How serious?: Critical (9.2 out of 10, both flaws). Does it reach you?: Check your stack (describe what you run and see what an attacker could reach in it). Are attackers trying?: Yes (millions of attempts, seen by one internet security company). Anyone confirmed hacked?: Not yet (no organisation, as of the latest check).

items.title: Front page: the core facts
items.text: There are two flaws. Both are in PHP itself, underneath every website that uses it, and both are rated critical: 9.2 out of 10. Someone anywhere on the internet, with no password, can use them against a website that has not installed the fix, and make its server run their own commands. Researchers proved this on the most traditional way of running PHP; for other setups it is likely but less certain.

items.title: Front page: what nobody knows yet
items.text: Whether any website was actually broken into before it installed the fix. Whether the fix is complete. A report on 21 October suggested it may not be; the PHP security team replied on the mailing list on 22 October, and this site will settle the question once that reply is saved here.

items.title: Front page: latest
items.text: 23 Oct, 10:03 UTC: Die Presse: as of 12:03 Vienna time (10:03 UTC) on 23 October no successful attack via the PHP flaws was known in Austria. 23 Oct, 09:16 UTC: Japan's RainForest reports that its honeypots recorded 21 php2shell-related requests from 14 different addresses: attempts, not break-ins.

items.text: A flaw is not a breach. items.title: Can anything be done to fix it, or do we just have to wait for updates?
items.text: The updates already exist: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 were released on 21 October and fix both flaws. Nobody is waiting on PHP; the wait is for whoever runs each server to install them and restart. If that is you, update now; if you cannot today, there are temporary settings and, as a last resort, taking the site offline. If a hosting company runs your site, ask them whether it is patched.

items.title: Is PHP really the software behind most websites?
items.text: Roughly, if you count websites, not the Internet. About 69% of the websites whose server-side language can be identified run PHP, and the share is falling; on every site the HTTP Archive crawls, PHP is detected on about half (the fact-check desk's investigation). Wiz's '70% of the Internet' is that website figure restated: nobody measures a share of 'the Internet'. Internet-facing PHP hosts number in the low millions: VulnCheck counts about 2.6 million, and Censys counted 1.57 million unpatched on 21 October among the 1.58 million whose version it could read.

items.title: Has anyone actually been hacked?
items.text: Not that any named organisation has said, as of 16:05 UTC on 24 October, the latest capture in the evidence vault. Attack attempts are real and in the millions at Cloudflare alone, Amazon saw one on a honeypot four days before disclosure, and two security vendors are reported as saying it is being exploited, without naming any victim (other reports of the same vendors describe attempts). CISA had not added it to its exploited-vulnerabilities list when last checked, and the sites that went offline say they did it as a precaution.

items.title: Do I need to change my passwords?
items.text: Not because of this, as things stand. The flaw is on web servers, not on your devices, and no named site has announced a breach through it, as of the latest check. If a site you use announces one, follow its instructions. Using a different password on every site is the protection that holds whatever the next flaw is.

items.title: How do I know whether my site is affected?
items.text: If the site runs on PHP (WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento, MediaWiki, and Laravel all do) and the running PHP version is older than 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 without a distribution backport, it is affected. Check the version where the code runs, after the restart, not the package list. For bought-in products, the Dutch NCSC keeps an inventory of 674 products and their status.

items.title: Should we take our site offline?
items.text: Only if you cannot patch or apply the temporary mitigations in time. That is the advice from the NSA, CISA and the UK NCSC, and it is the last step on every agency's list. If the site is patched and the workers restarted, the advice is to keep it up and watch it.

items.title: Why is this such big news?
items.text: Four things at once: the flaws are in PHP itself, which runs a large share of the web; they were found with AI help; the coordinated disclosure leaked a day early, so the fix shipped under pressure; and the NSA, CISA and NCSC told organisations that could not patch to take systems offline, which is why government, council and police sites went dark.

items.title: We are on PHP 7.4, 8.0 or 8.1. Is there a patch?
items.text: Not a release. PHP 8.1 and older are out of support; the project published source backport branches for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, which someone has to build. CISA says systems on 8.1 or older should be taken offline. Plan the migration to 8.2 or later now; in the meantime a distribution or vendor that backports, the temporary mitigations and isolation are the options.

items.title: We are behind Cloudflare (or another firewall). Are we safe?
items.text: Safer, not safe. Cloudflare's rules were live about nine hours before disclosure, on every plan including Free, and Akamai, Fastly, Imperva and Fortinet followed. Every one of them calls it a stopgap and says patch anyway: attackers mutate payloads, and the rules only see traffic that goes through the firewall.

items.title: Do our developers need to change our code?
items.text: No. Both bugs are in the C engine that runs PHP, not in PHP code, and the demonstrated attack runs before any application code. The fix is updating the PHP runtime and restarting it. What developers can do is check the version on the machines they deploy to and rebuild container images.

items.title: Patch at the speed of Metasploit: where php2shell sits on the weaponisation ladder, and the attacks that come second and third
items.text: A cyber desk's reading, 28 hours after the leak. php2shell is a serious engine bug with proven private exploits, but it has not become a one-request, works-everywhere exploit the way Log4Shell and Shellshock did. Here is the evidence for that, the ATT&CK path it would take, and the second and third stories (patching, testing, the response's own supply chain) that are likelier to hurt.
